_comment: Every tunable setting in Vessel is declared here, not in UI code. The
container editor renders this file with one composable per param type, so
adding a knob is a data change. Defaults are correct for the canoe target
and mirror build/targets/canoe.env.
'help' is shown next to the control. It must be one plain sentence that a
user who does not know what a translator is can act on. If a setting
cannot be explained that way, it does not belong in this file at all.
Nothing here is hidden any more: there is no 'advanced' flag and no
disclosure in the editor. That means ORDER IS THE HIERARCHY. Groups are
named for what a setting affects rather than for the subsystem that
implements it, and they run from the ones a user opens the screen for
(Display) to the ones that are correct until something breaks
(Compatibility). Put a new param where a user would look for it, not next
to the code that reads it.
For params of type 'component', the default is a selector, not a package
id: '@latest' resolves to the newest installed package of componentType.
Package ids are build outputs (dxvk-2.7.1-canoe) and must never be
hardcoded here, or a version bump would silently break every default.

groups.title: Display
groups.help: Desktop size, frame rate, and what opens on it.

params.title: Resolution
params.help: Lower is much faster, and it is the biggest dial on this phone: a game at 1280 x 720 measured 20-26 fps and the same scene at 640 x 360 hit the 60 fps cap. Halving each side quarters the pixels. Pick a size or type any WxH.

params.title: Frame rate limit
params.help: Only rates this screen can show. Lower keeps the phone cool.

groups.title: Graphics experiments
groups.help: Unproven. Each one is a question to measure, not a setting to leave on.
_comment: None of these has a measured effect on this device. They are here because
the stack is GPU-bound at 94-97% and the levers that could change that
were unreachable without a build. Every default below is the driver's own
behaviour, so a container nobody has touched runs exactly as it did.
Read docs/OPTIMIZATION.md before changing one, and change one at a time.
Absolute frame times do not survive between sessions on this phone -- the
same measurement moved 15% on thermal state alone -- so a comparison
across two launches is noise. TU_DEBUG_FILE (set automatically, under the
container's tmp/) lets a subset of the Turnip flags be switched while the
game runs, which is the only way to A/B these against the same scene at
the same temperature.

params.title: Tiling decision
params.help: Adreno can draw in on-chip tiles or straight to memory. The driver ships a rule that opts Direct3D games out of tiling entirely, so this game is almost certainly not tiling. 'bandwidth' is the driver's own rule, which weighs the memory traffic each way; 'profiled' times both and picks. To force one outright, use the gmem or sysmem flag under Diagnostics instead — those can also be switched while the game runs.
params._comment: prefer_gmem and prefer_sysmem were here and are gone. They are weaker than the TU_DEBUG flags of the same name -- a bias rather than a veto -- and unlike those they cannot be changed mid-session, which is the only way a tiling comparison on this device means anything. Two controls for one question, and this was the worse one.

params.title: Force tiles for busy passes
params.help: Draws a pass in tiles whenever it has ten or more draws. Metro averages about twenty a pass, so this flips most of them.

params.title: Overlap tile setup
params.help: Lets tile setup run alongside drawing. Off by default in the driver because it costs more than it saves on desktop games. Only means anything if the game is actually tiling.

params.title: Keep depth rejection through blending
params.help: Recovers early depth rejection that the driver gives up on after a blended draw. CAUTION: on a game that needs the caution, this renders incorrectly rather than crashing -- check the picture, not just the frame rate.

params.title: Per-pass GPU trace
params.help: Writes one record per render pass -- tiles or not, why depth rejection was dropped, and bytes moved -- to the container's tmp folder. Costs frame rate while it runs, so read the shape and not the fps.
params._comment: CSV rather than a choice of three. All of print/print_csv/print_json carry the same fields; only the encoding differs, and picking between them is not a decision anybody has information to make. CSV is the one a spreadsheet and a two-line script both open.

params.title: DXVK options
params.help: Passed straight to DXVK, one 'key = value' per line. Three worth trying, none proven: 'd3d11.cachedDynamicResources = a' (this phone shares memory between CPU and GPU, so the memory type DXVK avoids costs nothing here), 'd3d11.relaxedBarriers = True' and 'd3d11.relaxedGraphicsBarriers = True' (fewer forced breaks between draws).

groups.title: Compatibility
groups.help: One escape hatch for a single misbehaving program.

params.title: Extra DLL overrides
params.help: Wine's WINEDLLOVERRIDES. Leave empty unless following specific advice.

groups._fixedNote: Thread synchronisation is NOT a setting. It is fixed to esync, the only mode that works here, and the session launcher must set it unconditionally. ntsync needs a kernel driver Android does not ship on any branch and sepolicy would block anyway. fsync is worse than unavailable: Proton probes it with the futex_waitv syscall, which is absent from Android's seccomp allowlist, and the default action is SECCOMP_RET_TRAP — so the probe SIGSYS-kills the process instead of failing gracefully. Offering fsync in the UI would have shipped a crash. See README, Known limitations.
groups._note: The three FEX memory-ordering toggles (TSOEnabled, HalfBarrierTSOEnabled, VectorTSOEnabled) used to live here and are now fixed in SessionEnvironment.kt alongside WINEESYNC. They were removed for the same reason as the Settings, Components and GPU-drivers screens: every default was already the only correct one, and each was a trade a user would be making blind. Measured on this device (tools/tso/run.sh, and see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md 'Why memory ordering dominates on this chip'): strict ordering is required for correctness, the half-barrier path is a 21% win over disabling LRCPC2, and vector ordering is a severe cost that fixes nothing on hardware without FEAT_LRCPC3 codegen. Nothing a user could learn from the UI would change any of those. If a future device or FEX release changes the answer, the value changes in code -- it does not come back as a switch.
